touches.text: Trouble Ticket: an error that needs a non-automated fixer (CC or Akien).
In the event a second trouble is observed while the first is open, a new ticket is NEVER issued, we just increment a counter on the ticket.

A trouble has a point of origin, and that is how we match them up. When raised with a condition, its emission source AND error message are checked against open tickets. If found, increment the counter; either way, pass the ticket back to the caller.
The incrementing is part of the trouble ticket class.
So the error a raiser reports is the same words every time it happens; whatever changes from one time to the next (a pid, a timestamp, a temp path) goes in the details, not the error.
Trouble Tickets are disposable artifacts once closed. They are file artifacts, live in the logging tree, and are cleared out on a 30 day cycle by the cairn device during a sleep cycle.
Trouble tickets live inside the recovery device (7.3.4), since recovery has to work when other things don't.
Everything held for seconds to days lives here: mail, logs, test runs, trouble tickets, inference tickets.

The transient tree is for things that may help debugging out to 30 days and won't be needed past that, eg an inference ticket looked at a week later because a bug turned up. No trouble should stand unresolved at 30 days; sleep's cleanup may be made to spare one that does. (Q#8, Akien 2026-11-03)
Trouble tickets (3.3.3) live here. Any device has a direct line to raise one, not over the bus (2.2.8.1.3).
TESTER MACHINE, CodeMother's (was the tester device, cairn/devices/tester/)
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.
Notices: what a run saw that nobody asked about, surfaced to the operator.
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).
